headline: 100 g·h⁻¹ of carbohydrate kept cyclists' 15-min power up better than 60 g·h⁻¹ after 4 h, with no glycogen difference
question: Does taking 100 g of carbohydrate per hour instead of 60 g during a long ride protect performance late on (durability), and does it do so by sparing muscle glycogen?
design: A randomised, double-blind crossover trial in 15 trained male cyclists and triathletes. Each did a 15-minute time trial fresh, then a 4 h prolonged intermittent cycling session (240 min at 60% of fresh 15-min mean power, with high-intensity intervals) and repeated the time trial. They ate a carbohydrate-rich diet for 24 h first. In one visit they took 60 g·h⁻¹ (CHO60) and in the other 100 g·h⁻¹ (CHO100), as drinks and gels with glucose to fructose in a 1:0.8 ratio. Muscle biopsies from the vastus lateralis before and after measured glycogen, and gas exchange measured whole-body carbohydrate burning.
findings:
After 4 h, 15-min time-trial power fell 9.3 ± 2.0% with CHO60 and 6.4 ± 1.7% with CHO100 (P = 0.025). Mean power was 9 W higher with CHO100 (P = 0.028).

Muscle glycogen fell a lot in both and ended similar: 192 ± 99 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry mass (CHO60) vs 209 ± 111 (CHO100), P = 0.56. Whole-body carbohydrate burning held up better with CHO100 (2.6 to 2.3 g·min⁻¹ vs 2.6 to 1.9 g·min⁻¹ with CHO60, P = 0.047). Blood glucose stayed steady in both (about 5.6 to 6.1 mmol·L⁻¹).
limits: Only 15 men, all trained, so the result may not carry to women or less trained people. "Without altering glycogen utilization" in the title is stronger than the data: with standard deviations of about 100 mmol·kg⁻¹ dry mass in 15 people, a modest difference cannot be ruled out. Glycogen was measured only before and after, in whole muscle, so changes during the ride or in single fibres are missed. The 9 W gain is a 3-point smaller drop in a lab time trial after a fixed 4 h protocol; a race is different. The abstract reports no gut-comfort data, and riders may not all tolerate 100 g·h⁻¹. The full paper is not open, and Europe PMC, Crossref and OpenAlex list no funder or conflict-of-interest statement, so funding and conflicts could not be checked. A single crossover trial is weak evidence.
meaning: The fuelling lessons (fuel-during) teach 30–60 g·h⁻¹ for 1–2.5 h and up to 90 g·h⁻¹ for longer efforts, using glucose plus fructose, and show a dose curve where gains flatten above about 78 g·h⁻¹. fuel-transportable notes that 100–120 g·h⁻¹ raises carbohydrate burning but that whether it makes you faster is still open. This trial adds one controlled test where 100 g·h⁻¹ protected late-ride power better than 60 g·h⁻¹, in line with the durability lesson (dur-training), where critical power after 3 h fell less with 120 than with 60 g·h⁻¹. The surprise is the mechanism: end glycogen was no different, so the gain may come from keeping carbohydrate burning up rather than from sparing glycogen. It does not overturn any lesson: one small trial in men, and it did not test 80–90 g·h⁻¹, the usual upper advice.

variants.stem: In the 2026 trial, cyclists rode 4 h and then did a 15-min time trial. With 60 g·h⁻¹ their power fell 9.3%. What happened with 100 g·h⁻¹?

options.text: It fell less, by 6.4%, so late-ride power was better kept
options.why: Right: the drop was 6.4% with CHO100 vs 9.3% with CHO60 (P = 0.025), about 9 W more power.

options.text: It fell more, since extra carbohydrate upsets the gut
options.why: Power was better kept with CHO100; gut upset was not the finding.

options.text: It did not change, because both groups ended with the same glycogen
options.why: The glycogen was similar but performance still differed.

options.text: It rose above the fresh value
options.why: Both conditions were below the fresh time trial (−9.3% and −6.4%).

variants.stem: A cyclist plans a 5 h ride and trains the gut to take 100 g·h⁻¹ instead of 60 g·h⁻¹. Based on the 2026 trial, what is the most reasonable expectation for his late-ride power?

options.text: A smaller late-ride drop in power, if his gut copes with the rate
options.why: Right: in 15 male cyclists a 100 g·h⁻¹ intake gave a smaller drop in 15-min power after 4 h.

options.text: A faster start, since carbohydrate matters only early on
options.why: The benefit showed late in the ride, in the final time trial.

options.text: No effect, since glycogen use was the same in both trials
options.why: Equal glycogen did not mean equal performance.

options.text: A guaranteed gain for every rider, whatever the gut
options.why: The study was 15 men; individual gut limits were not tested.

variants.stem: Muscle glycogen at the end was about the same with 60 and 100 g·h⁻¹, yet power was better with 100. What does this suggest?

options.text: The benefit may come from steadier carbohydrate burning, not glycogen sparing
options.why: Right: whole-body carbohydrate oxidation fell to 2.3 g·min⁻¹ with CHO100 vs 1.9 g·min⁻¹ with CHO60, while end glycogen did not differ (P = 0.56).

options.text: The biopsies must have been wrong
options.why: Equal glycogen is a result, not a sign of error; the study measured it directly.

options.text: Extra carbohydrate saved glycogen in the working muscle
options.why: The trial found no difference in glycogen use (P = 0.56).

options.text: Blood glucose crashed less in the 100 g condition
options.why: Blood glucose stayed stable over time in both conditions (about 5.6 to 6.1 mmol·L⁻¹).

variants.stem: What most limits how far the 2026 100 vs 60 g·h⁻¹ result applies to a typical runner or cyclist?

options.text: Only 15 trained men were tested in one lab protocol
options.why: Right: with n = 15 and trained men only, the finding is weak evidence and may not hold for women or others.

options.text: The trial was not randomised
options.why: It was a randomised, double-blind crossover trial.

options.text: Participants knew which carbohydrate dose they got
options.why: The design was double-blind.

options.text: Muscle glycogen was not measured
options.why: It was measured, by biopsy, before and after the ride.

variants.stem: Each cyclist did both the 60 and the 100 g·h⁻¹ visit. What does this crossover design do for the result?

options.text: Each rider is his own control, which reduces noise between people
options.why: Right: comparing the same person on both doses removes much person-to-person variation.

options.text: It guarantees the result applies to all athletes
options.why: A crossover helps within the group; it does not widen who the group is.

options.text: It makes blinding unnecessary
options.why: The trial was also double-blind; a crossover does not replace it.

options.text: It lets the study measure performance without a fresh baseline
options.why: The trial used a fresh time trial as its baseline.
